question: Molecular mimicry — where a microbial antigen structurally resembles a self-antigen — is the mechanism by which rheumatic heart disease develops after Group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is actually true. Molecular mimicry is indeed the mechanism behind rheumatic heart disease. Anti-streptococcal antibodies (particularly against M-protein) cross-react with cardiac myosin because streptococcal M-protein shares structural epitopes with heart tissue proteins. This is a textbook example of molecular mimicry — distinct from immune complex disease, which involves deposition of circulating antigen–antibody complexes.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. In molecular mimicry, antibodies and T cells generated against streptococcal M-protein cross-react with cardiac myosin and valve glycoproteins because the microbial and self-antigens share structural epitopes. This autoimmune cross-reaction drives the carditis of rheumatic heart disease — a classic example of post-infectious autoimmunity and one of the most important causes of acquired heart disease in young Indians.
